title: Cash-Out Refinance vs. HELOC: Tapping Your Home Equity
description: Cash-out refinance or HELOC? Compare cost, flexibility, and what happens to your existing mortgage before you tap your Southern California home equity.
image_alt: A bright white kitchen with cabinets and a window

faq.q: What's the main difference between a cash-out refinance and a HELOC?
faq.a: A cash-out refinance replaces your current mortgage with a new, larger one and gives you the difference in cash. A HELOC is a separate line of credit on top of your existing mortgage.

faq.q: Which is better if I have a low rate on my current mortgage?
faq.a: Many homeowners with a low existing rate prefer a HELOC or home equity loan so they can keep their first mortgage untouched. The right answer depends on the amounts and your plans.

faq.q: Is interest on home equity debt tax-deductible?
faq.a: In some cases, depending on how the money is used and current tax law. Check with a tax professional for your situation.

body_html:
Southern California homeowners have built substantial equity over the past several years. When it's time to remodel, consolidate debt, or fund a big life expense, the question becomes how to access that equity without making a costly mistake.

The two most common tools are a cash-out refinance and a home equity line of credit, or HELOC. They solve the same problem in very different ways.

How each one works

Cash-out refinance: You replace your current mortgage with a new, larger loan and receive the difference in cash at closing. You end up with one loan and one payment, at whatever terms the new loan carries.

HELOC: You keep your existing mortgage and add a separate line of credit secured by your home. You draw what you need, when you need it, during the draw period, and you typically pay interest only on what you've used.

Side by side

Cash-out refinanceHELOC
Your first mortgageReplaced with a new loanStays exactly as it is
How you get the moneyLump sum at closingDraw as needed
Rate typeFixed or adjustable optionsUsually variable
Closing costsSimilar to a full refinanceOften lower
Best forLarge, one-time needs or improving your overall loanProjects that unfold over time or uncertain amounts

The question that usually decides it

What's the rate on your current mortgage, and how much do you need? If your existing first mortgage has favorable terms, a cash-out refinance means giving those up on the entire balance, not just the new money. In that case, a HELOC or fixed home equity loan often makes more sense, because you only pay new-market pricing on the amount you borrow.

On the other hand, if your current rate isn't especially attractive, or you need a large amount and want a fixed payment, a cash-out refinance can simplify everything into one loan.

Smart uses and risky uses

  • Often smart: renovations that add livability or value, consolidating high-interest debt with a clear payoff plan, an ADU that could create rental income
  • Proceed carefully: vacations, vehicles, or investments where you could lose the money

Remember that both options are secured by your home. Rolling credit card debt into your mortgage can lower your monthly obligations, but only helps if the cards stay paid down afterward.

What lenders look at

  1. Combined loan-to-value. How much you'd owe in total compared to your home's value.
  2. Credit and income. You still need to qualify for the new payment.
  3. Property type and occupancy. Primary residences get the most options.

Home equity loans: the third option

There's another tool worth mentioning: the fixed home equity loan, sometimes called a second mortgage. Like a HELOC, it leaves your first mortgage untouched. Unlike a HELOC, you receive the money as a lump sum and repay it with fixed payments. It's a good fit when you know exactly how much you need and want payment certainty, but don't want to give up your first mortgage's terms.

  • Choose a HELOC when costs will come in over time, like a remodel paid in stages
  • Choose a home equity loan when you need a set amount and prefer a fixed payment
  • Choose a cash-out refinance when replacing your first mortgage also makes sense on its own

Questions to ask before you borrow

  1. How will the rate adjust on a variable HELOC, and is there a cap?
  2. What happens when the HELOC draw period ends and repayment begins?
  3. Are there annual fees, minimum draws, or early closure fees?
  4. How much equity will I have left as a cushion after borrowing?
  5. If home values dip, could my line be reduced or frozen?

That last question matters. Lenders can sometimes reduce or freeze a HELOC if property values fall significantly. If you're counting on the line for a project, draw funds as you need them and have a backup plan.

The takeaway

A cash-out refinance reshapes your whole mortgage. A HELOC adds flexible borrowing on top of the mortgage you already have. Compare both with real numbers based on your current loan, and be clear about what the money is for. If you're weighing a full refinance anyway, read when refinancing actually makes sense first.
